text: You get the root of a binary tree. Return the values of its nodes in inorder.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — inorder means: for every node, I visit the whole left subtree first, then the node itself, then the whole right subtree. So the rule is the same at every node, all the way down. Is that right?

Then here's the thing I want to name up front, because it shapes the whole solution. A binary tree isn't really nodes with three shapes — root, inner node, leaf. It's nodes plus empty links; a leaf is just a node whose two children are both empty. If I treat empty as the floor of the recursion, I never need a special case for a leaf. That one choice removes every branch I'd otherwise have to write.
Can the tree be empty — can root be null?
Yes. An empty tree should return an empty list.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to one hundred nodes, values between minus one hundred and one hundred. The tree can be any shape.

Good — a hundred is small, so even a fully skewed chain is safe for recursion. Let me run through the example: one, null, two, three. Node one is the root with no left child; its right child is two, and two has a left child, three. One's left is empty, so I record one first. Then inside two, the left subtree comes first, so three goes before two. The answer is one, three, two. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to handle each node shape by hand: a leaf, only a left child, only a right child, both. That's four cases per node, and every one is a place to get it wrong — and it doesn't get faster, just longer. This problem reminds me of a plain depth-first search on a tree. The definition of inorder is already recursive — left, node, right — so the code can be a direct copy of the definition. I'll use recursion with an output vector I pass down and fill in place.

Here's the plan. One: if the node is empty, return. Two: recurse into the left subtree. Three: push the node's value, then recurse into the right subtree. One shared vector holds the answer; each call only appends to its end. One thing worth flagging — the empty check isn't a speed guard, it's the base case. If I wrote the floor as a leaf check instead, two things break: an empty tree crashes reading root's left, and every leaf returns before its push, so leaf values are silently dropped. An explicit stack would avoid recursion, but with a hundred nodes the call stack isn't a risk. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The public function creates the answer vector, calls the helper on the root, and returns it. The helper is three lines after the null check — left, push, right — matching the plan line for line. One thing worth flagging — the ampersand on the vector parameter is a correctness detail, not a speed detail. Drop it and every call gets its own private copy: the pushes land in that copy, the copy dies at the end of the call, and the outer answer is never touched. So every non-empty tree would return an empty list, while the empty tree still passes — exactly the kind of bug that looks fine on the first test.

Let's dry-run the code. One, null, two, three — I expect one, three, two. The row that matters is the first push: node one doesn't push when it's first reached, only after its left side is fully done — here that's a single call on an empty link. Seven calls in total: three real nodes and four empty links. That matches. Corner cases: an empty tree returns an empty list at once. A single node gives its value, with no leaf case anywhere. A left chain, three, two, one, pushes on the way back up, giving one, two, three, the deepest shape.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear, and exactly so: every node and every empty link is entered once. A tree with n nodes has n plus one empty links — two n child slots, and n minus one hold a real node. So it's exactly two n plus one calls, whatever the shape: seven in our run. Space is order h for the call stack, where h is the height. The output vector is the answer itself, so I don't count it as extra. Worst case is a chain, where h equals n. At a hundred nodes that's fine; at a million, the chain would overflow the stack, and I'd switch to an explicit stack. Oh, one more thing — the traversal never writes to the tree, so it's safe to rerun.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed the empty link as the base case up front, and showed the leaf-check version both crashes on an empty tree and drops every leaf — a correctness argument, not a style note. You called out that the ampersand on the vector is required, and named the exact wrong output. And you derived the exact call count, two n plus one, from the empty-link count, then split space into the call stack versus the output. Good work.
